about.title: Real conspiracies and unproven ones: how people weigh evidence
about.length_note: About 35 minutes. Four short case studies, two thinking habits, one thought experiment and a five-step checklist fit in that time with pauses for the questions. Each section stands alone, so you can stop and resume between sections.

say.text: Welcome. Today's idea: big events are secretly arranged by hidden groups. Where this idea stands: popular speculation, when it is used as a blanket explanation.

show.text: Where this idea stands: popular speculation

say.text: Hold on. Conspiracies do happen, don't they?

show.text: Conspiracies do happen

say.text: They do. That is the accepted view. Some conspiracies are real and documented, and each claim has to stand on its own evidence.

show.text: Accepted view: real conspiracies exist | Each claim is judged on its own evidence

say.text: Plenty of thoughtful people hold these beliefs. They are found across all parts of society. Nobody here is being mocked.

show.text: "Not everyone who believes in a conspiracy is unreasonable or unthinking." Dr David Robert Grimes

say.text: First, a plain definition. In law, a conspiracy is two or more people who agree to break the law, and then take a step to act on it.

show.text: Conspiracy = agreement + a step taken

ask.q: In law, what two things make a conspiracy?
ask.right: An agreement by two or more people, and a step taken to carry it out
wrong: One person's secret wish, and a rumour that others repeat
A big event, and no obvious cause
A plan that was never discussed with anyone
ask.why: The agreement is the heart of it, but talk alone is not enough. Someone must take a step after the agreement.

say.text: A 'conspiracy theory' is something different. It is a claim that a secret plot by several people explains an event.

show.text: Conspiracy theory = a claim that a secret plot explains an event

say.text: So a claim becomes a documented conspiracy only when evidence backs it. Many grand claims are hard to test, and some have little evidence behind them.

show.text: Documented conspiracy: records, recordings, court findings | Unsupported theory: hard to test, little evidence

say.text: Let's watch real ones come to light. Four cases. Notice what kind of evidence each one needed.

show.text: Four real cases

say.text: Case one: Watergate. On the night of June 17, 1972, five burglars broke into the Democratic National Committee offices in Washington.

show.text: Five burglars

say.text: Investigators followed the trail of abuses to the highest levels of the Nixon administration, and in the end to the President himself.

show.text: A trail that led to the top

say.text: Part of it was a plan to mislead. Nixon ordered the CIA to ask the FBI to call off its investigation, as if the break-in were a national security matter.

show.text: Misleading the FBI

say.text: The key evidence was Nixon's own recordings. In July 1973, a Senate hearing learned that a secret taping system had recorded his conversations.

show.text: Secret tapes

say.text: Nixon wanted those tapes kept secret. The Supreme Court later ordered them handed over, and he resigned on August 9, 1974.

show.text: June 17, 1972: break-in | July 1973: tapes revealed | July 1974: Supreme Court orders tapes handed over | August 9, 1974: Nixon resigns

ask.q: What finally settled the Watergate cover-up?
ask.right: Recordings and records obtained through investigations and a court order
wrong: An anonymous letter nobody could check
A feeling that the event was too big to be an accident
The president's falling popularity
ask.why: Real evidence did the work: the tapes and the court-ordered records. A hunch that the event was big did not.

say.text: Case two: Volkswagen. Engineers wrote software that could tell when a car was being emissions-tested, so the car could cheat the test.

show.text: Software that cheated emissions tests

say.text: This affected hundreds of thousands of diesel cars. The Justice Department described a conspiracy that lasted nearly ten years.

show.text: Nearly 10 years

say.text: It came out through outside testing. A study published in spring 2014 found a gap between test and road results. In 2015, Volkswagen admitted it had installed defeat devices.

show.text: Outside testing found the gap

say.text: The company later pleaded guilty to three felonies, including conspiracy to defraud the United States. An engineer pleaded guilty and agreed to cooperate.

show.text: Guilty pleas

say.text: Case three: the Gulf of Tonkin, 1964. The U.S. said its ships were attacked twice. The National Security Agency's own declassified history confirms there was no second attack, on August 4.

show.text: No second attack

say.text: That claim was used to support air strikes and a Congressional resolution that gave the White House freedom of action in Vietnam.

show.text: A claim that carried real weight

say.text: So it was a plot to start a war?

show.text: Plot, or mistake kept alive?

say.text: Careful. The agency's historian found no smoking gun of a cover-up. He did find signs of an effort to make the intelligence fit the claim. Documented does not mean fully explained.

show.text: Documented: the attack did not happen | Still argued: how deliberate the misreporting was

say.text: Case four: MKUltra. It was a closely held CIA research project that ran from 1953 to 1964.

show.text: MKUltra: a closely held CIA project

say.text: Its code name became public in 1975 during the Rockefeller Commission and Church Committee investigations. In 1977 the CIA reported finding seven more boxes of documents.

show.text: 1953: project begins | 1975: becomes public | 1977: seven boxes of documents reported

say.text: Four cases, four routes into the open. Look for the pattern.

show.text: Recordings plus a court order (Watergate) | Outside testing plus an insider's guilty plea (Volkswagen) | A declassified internal study (Gulf of Tonkin) | Official investigations plus records found later (MKUltra)

say.text: Here is roughly how long each took to be officially confirmed. These are rounded.

show.text: Years until official records confirmed each case (rounded)

say.text: But you only know about the secrets that failed. What about the ones that never leaked?

show.text: We only see the exposed ones

say.text: That is a fair point, and a real limit. Real cases show conspiracies exist. They can't tell us how many hidden ones there are, or whether a particular claim is one.

show.text: Real cases prove possible, not probable

ask.q: Which of these is a documented conspiracy?
ask.right: The Watergate cover-up, shown by tapes, court records and testimony
wrong: A hidden group runs everything, but no records have ever been found
Everything bad that happens was planned by someone
This event was so huge that someone must have planned it
ask.why: A documented conspiracy rests on checkable evidence. The other three are claims with nothing checkable behind them.

say.text: Now the mind. Why do some theories feel so convincing? Two habits first, then a third.

show.text: Why theories feel convincing

say.text: Habit one: pattern-seeking. In six experiments, people who felt out of control saw more patterns, even among random or unrelated things.

show.text: Pattern-seeking

say.text: Feeling out of control is very human. The same research suggests that feeling more secure and in control can reduce the habit.

show.text: Feeling secure helps

ask.q: In those experiments, what happened when people felt a loss of control?
ask.right: They saw more patterns, even in random things
wrong: They stopped noticing patterns
They only noticed patterns that were really there
Nothing changed
ask.why: Lacking control increased illusory pattern perception. In other words, people saw meaning in random or unrelated things.

say.text: Habit two: big events seem to need big causes. Psychologists call it proportionality bias.

show.text: Big event, big cause

say.text: In one study, people read about an attack on a president. More of them chose a conspiracy explanation when the president died than when he survived.

show.text: President survived: fewer conspiracy answers | President died: more conspiracy answers

say.text: Two cautions. This is one possible influence, not the whole story. And a large outcome can have a simple cause, so check the evidence itself.

show.text: One influence, not the whole story

ask.q: Two people read about a car crash involving a political leader. One reads that the leader died, the other that the leader survived. Who is more likely to suspect a plot?
ask.right: The reader who was told the leader died
wrong: The reader who was told the leader survived
Both the same, every time
Neither, because people never suspect plots
ask.why: In studies like this, a bigger outcome made people more ready to accept a bigger cause.

say.text: Habit three: distrust. After Watergate, being wary of officials is reasonable. The habit to watch is when distrust replaces evidence, instead of asking for it.

show.text: Distrust: ask for evidence, don't swap it

say.text: Thought experiment time. How many people can keep a secret?

show.text: Thought experiment: how many people can keep a secret?

say.text: Picture a secret known to one person. Now two. Now a thousand. Each extra person is one more chance for it to slip out, on purpose or by accident.

show.text: Each person is another chance to leak

say.text: Physicist David Grimes turned that idea into an equation. It covers a whistle-blower telling on purpose, or a bungler giving it away by accident. Large conspiracies quickly became untenable.

show.text: Whistle-blowers and bunglers

say.text: He tried it on a claim that the Moon landings were faked. His estimate was that it would have leaked in about three years and eight months. We'll look at that case in class ten.

show.text: 3 years 8 months

ask.q: In this thought experiment, what makes a secret more likely to leak?
ask.right: More people in on it, and more time passing
wrong: Fewer people in on it
A bigger event
Nothing: secrets leak at the same rate whatever the size
ask.why: The model's chance of a leak grows with the number of people and the number of years.

say.text: But MKUltra stayed secret for decades. Doesn't that break the model?

show.text: Secrets that lasted

say.text: Fair. It's a model built on estimated leak rates, not a proof. It says small, tight groups can last a long time, and it can't judge any one claim alone.

show.text: A model is an estimate, not a verdict

say.text: Now the checklist. Five questions to ask before you weigh any claim. First two.

show.text: 1. What exactly is claimed, and could it be tested? | 2. What is the evidence: records, recordings, court findings?

say.text: Next two. Leave the page and see what other trusted sources say. Then ask how many people would need to keep quiet, and for how long.

show.text: 3. What do other trusted sources say? | 4. How many people, for how many years?

say.text: Last one. Is there a simpler explanation? And what would change my mind? Judge the evidence, not how big the event feels.

show.text: 5. Is there a simpler explanation, and what would change my mind?

say.text: Let's try it on an invented claim: a secret club of 3,000 people has quietly arranged every traffic light in a country for 30 years. No documents have been found.

show.text: An invented claim to test

ask.q: Which checklist questions flag the biggest problem with that claim?
ask.right: How many people for how long (3,000 for 30 years), and what evidence exists (none found)
wrong: Only that the claim sounds unusual
Only that traffic lights are boring
None: the claim passes every question
ask.why: A large group keeping quiet for decades, with no documents, fails questions two and four. Unusual-sounding is not the test. Evidence and plausibility are.

say.text: To wrap up: real conspiracies exist, and evidence is what shows them. Minds love patterns and big causes, so slow down and use the checklist.

show.text: Documented conspiracy = evidence you can check | Habits: pattern-seeking, big event/big cause, distrust | Tool: the five-question checklist

ask.q: Which habit says 'a huge event needs a huge cause'?
wrong: Lateral reading
An overt act
A defeat device
ask.why: Proportionality bias is the tendency to expect a big event to have a big cause. Lateral reading is a checking tool, an overt act is a legal step, and a defeat device was Volkswagen's cheating software.

notes.topic: How many people can keep a secret?

other_side.claim: Large secrets leak quickly, so grand conspiracies are very unlikely (the Grimes model).
other_side.other_view: The model depends on estimated leak rates and is not proof about any one claim. Some philosophers (called particularists) say each theory should be judged on its own evidence rather than by general odds. Real cases such as MKUltra stayed hidden for about two decades.

other_side.claim: The Gulf of Tonkin misreporting was a deliberate cover-up.
other_side.other_view: The NSA historian found no smoking gun of a cover-up, though he saw an active effort to make intelligence fit the claim. Historian John Prados argues that the story was in effect created inside the Defense Department and the Navy. How deliberate it was is still argued.

other_side.claim: Proportionality bias explains why people believe conspiracy theories.
other_side.other_view: It is one possible influence, not a full explanation of anyone's beliefs. Big outcomes can have complex causes, so the question is always what the evidence supports.

other_side.claim: Because real conspiracies exist, unproven ones deserve equal weight.
other_side.other_view: Real cases show conspiracies are possible. They don't show a particular claim is true, and we only see the ones that were exposed. Particularists would say judge each claim on its own merits.
